scenes.title: Cold open
narration: On August 1st, a performer dons a shishi mask to embody the mountain deity of Mount Hayachine, concluding a five-hour cycle of twelve ritual dances that have been performed since the 14th or 15th century.
This is Hayachine Kagura. 14th-15th century.
on_screen: Title card: Hayachine Kagura · Japan · 14th-15th century

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The tradition originated in the 14th or 15th century in the Iwate Prefecture, rooted in the worship of Mount Hayachine.
It was historically performed by shrine officers and is believed to have been influenced by the practices of yamabushi, mountain-dwelling Buddhist ascetics.
Scholars continue to investigate its potential links to the history of Noh theater.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The dances are performed in honor of Seoritsu, the tutelary deity of Mount Hayachine.
The performance serves to demonstrate the power of the mountain deity, bless the people, and reconfirm the identity of the community.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Performers wear masks during the dances.
The primary setting is the Hayachine Shrine in Hanamaki, Iwate, where the performance takes place on August 1st, though it is also performed in other locations.

scenes.title: The people
narration: While the main tradition is at Hayachine Shrine, 'discipleship' shows are performed throughout the Iwate Prefecture, though rarely as the full twelve-dance cycle.
The tradition is a type of Kagura, a category of ritual dance in Shinto ceremonies.
